extracted.intended_audience: reporters and journalism students covering local/municipal news and feature writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and treating miscellaneous local-news items (municipal institutions, schools, libraries, museums, business items and short entertaining sketches of city life), including purpose, treatment, and examples of effective leads and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of miscellaneous local stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal forms: (1) timely, significant information about public institutions and business activities (schools, public libraries, museums, parks, departments of city government, real estate, manufacturing, business); (2) entertaining feature stories — little incidents or sketches of daily city life that have no great news significance but amuse or interest readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which form a local item belongs to before reporting/writing. The former serves civic information needs; the latter aims to entertain with human-interest glimpses (including animals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — informative vs. entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative class aims to furnish timely, significant information in attractive form concerning public institutions and business activities. The entertaining class aims to amuse or give glimpses of city life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive journalism should stimulate citizen interest in municipal affairs by periodically presenting significant information about public institutions; entertaining pieces should still respect truth and the newspaper's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost accuracy in presenting information of public affairs and business matters is absolutely essential. The same standard of truthfulness must be maintained in entertaining feature stories; newspapers must not present anything in their news columns that is not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictitious details are never justifiable in news or feature stories. Maintain rigorous fact-checking even when the story is written primarily to entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — lead with striking facts or unusual statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking facts and figures or unusual statements, featured at the beginning, catch the reader's eye and lead him to read the story as long as its subject matter and style interest him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an attention-grabbing opening (statistic, bold comparison, or surprising statement). Examples cited: 'Public Schools Open', 'School for Backward-Children', 'New Feature in Manufacturing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of statistics and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statistics and comparisons to make institutional and business stories interesting and to illustrate significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature striking numeric comparisons early (e.g., comparing school enrollment to army sizes) to provide scale and context; ensure statistics are accurate and sourced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrative and literary devices in entertaining features
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative and descriptive beginnings, conversation, suspense, humor, and other devices used in short stories and novels are well adapted to entertaining local-news sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the goal is entertainment (not hard news), employ storytelling techniques — scene-setting, dialogue, suspense — while still avoiding invention or fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading instruction — five focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Five points for special attention in school reading instruction: (1) Correct pronunciation of words at an acceptable rate of speed; (2) Expression of the meaning of what is read; (3) Distinct reading; (4) Pleasing use of the voice; (5) Ability to get the meaning of what is read silently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silent reading ability should be emphasized as it develops reasoning; these five points are used to shape curricula and contests/assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and rules for school reading contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules and scheduling for reading contests: repeat successful plans, hold two series during the school year (one concluded by Dec. 23, another in late March), inter-district readings April 25–June 1, each school sends one reader and one alternate, each child allowed three minutes for reading a familiar section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No centralized arrangement required for trained readers; encourage cooperation with colleges of reading; include sight reading and brief silent-reading tests at inter-district events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading diagnostic/testing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for diagnosing poor reading: give graded prose/poetry/oratory, comprehension questions, reproduction tasks; record time and error counts; use darkened projection with phonograph recording, camera for eye movements, breathing instrument; use blackout of projected text to test recall beyond the visible word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep careful timing/error records; combine subjective teacher reports with objective machine-assisted measures to identify causes of poor reading and possible remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and curriculum design for vocational/reform schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocational schools should provide industrial training to improve a boy's chance in the world; bridewell vocational schools for prisoners aim to reclaim offenders by giving them skills to avoid relapse into crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses to match practical employment needs (example Pullman Free School courses: cabinet work, pattern-making, blacksmithing, foundry work, machine-shop work, electric construction, steam/electric operating, engineering, English, mathematics, drawing, household arts & sciences). Consider open accessibility rules set by bequests/trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education for backward children — separate classes and expert instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many retarded children can be helped by separate classes and expert teachers; only a small number of mental defectives belong in institutions, while the largest percent of retarded children could be rescued by special training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School boards should survey and plan separate classrooms and specialist teachers; early intervention can prevent later social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical inspection of schoolchildren — uniformity and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical inspection as practiced was found unsatisfactory: no uniformity in methods, great variation in time spent by physicians (five minutes to 1.5 hours), and in numbers of children examined (from none to thirty); examinations for physical defects were incomplete and not consistently followed by results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend a more definite method of examination, consistent procedures, adequate coverage, and consideration of establishing a department of school hygiene to centralize control and standards; use principals' and superintendent reports to assess adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public library disease-prevention practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Library cooperation with health authorities to prevent disease spread: daily lists of homes with contagious disease, removal and mailing of identifying cards for books from such homes, fumigation of books returned from infected houses, and fumigation of books when health department clears a house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While routine fumigation of all circulating books is not practiced, libraries should coordinate with health departments and take targeted precautions for books from known contagion sites; note differing opinions about the risk of disease transmission by books.
